en_de_m2_articles.helpMemoryIntro: Give each noun its gender. There is no fool-proof rule, so the goal is to learn the article as part of the word.

helpMemoryTips.title: Three genders, one habit
helpMemoryTips.text: Every noun has a gender: **der** (m), **die** (f), **das** (n). Always learn the noun *with* its article — **der** Tisch, **die** Lampe, **das** Buch.

helpMemoryTips.title: Endings that betray the gender
helpMemoryTips.text: → **die**: -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, and most -e words. → **das**: -chen, -lein, -ment, -um. → **der**: -er (doer/tool), -ig, -ling, -or.

helpMemoryTips.title: ein / eine / kein
helpMemoryTips.text: Nominative: **ein** (m/n), **eine** (f). Negate a noun with kein: **kein** Hund (m), **keine** Zeit (f), **kein** Auto (n), **keine** Kinder (pl).

helpMemoryTips.title: der/die/das = er/sie/es
helpMemoryTips.text: In the nominative the article echoes the pronoun: der → **er**, die → **sie**, das → **es**.

helpMemoryTips.title: Endings beat meaning
helpMemoryTips.text: **das** Mädchen and **das** Kind are neuter because of the noun (-chen, das Kind), not the person. Grammar wins over logic.

en_de_m2_bigtext.readingPassage: Das ist ein Foto von meiner verrückten Familie! Der Mann ganz links ist mein Vater. Er ist Polizist und sehr streng, aber zu Hause kocht er am liebsten und singt dabei furchtbar laut. Die Frau neben ihm ist meine Mutter. Sie ist Ärztin und meistens ruhig — nur wenn mein Vater singt, lacht sie und schüttelt den Kopf. Das Mädchen mit der roten Brille bin ich. Der Junge daneben ist mein kleiner Bruder; das Kind isst den ganzen Tag und träumt nur vom Fußball. Hinten seht ihr das Haus mit dem grünen Dach — dort wohnen wir alle zusammen. Der Garten ist winzig, aber meine Mutter liebt ihn über alles. Und der Hund? Der Hund heißt Bello, frisst heimlich die Hausschuhe und ist trotzdem der König der Familie. Habt ihr auch ein Haustier? Wir haben übrigens noch eine Katze, aber sie mag den frechen Bello überhaupt nicht!
en_de_m2_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: This is a photo of my crazy family! The man on the far left is my father. He is a police officer and very strict, but at home he loves cooking most of all and sings terribly loudly while he does. The woman next to him is my mother. She is a doctor and usually calm — only when my father sings does she laugh and shake her head. The girl with the red glasses is me. The boy next to me is my little brother; the child eats all day and dreams only of football. At the back you can see the house with the green roof — that is where we all live together. The garden is tiny, but my mother loves it more than anything. And the dog? The dog is called Bello, secretly eats the slippers, and is still the king of the family. Do you have a pet too? By the way, we also have a cat, but she doesn't like cheeky Bello at all!

en_de_m2_pronouns.helpMemoryIntro: The subject pronouns. German "sie" does triple duty — she, they, and (capitalised) the formal "you" — so context and the verb tell them apart.

helpMemoryTips.title: Three genders, one habit
helpMemoryTips.text: Every noun has a gender: **der** (m), **die** (f), **das** (n). Always learn the noun *with* its article — **der** Tisch, **die** Lampe, **das** Buch.

helpMemoryTips.title: Endings that betray the gender
helpMemoryTips.text: → **die**: -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, and most -e words. → **das**: -chen, -lein, -ment, -um. → **der**: -er (doer/tool), -ig, -ling, -or.

helpMemoryTips.title: ein / eine / kein
helpMemoryTips.text: Nominative: **ein** (m/n), **eine** (f). Negate a noun with kein: **kein** Hund (m), **keine** Zeit (f), **kein** Auto (n), **keine** Kinder (pl).

helpMemoryTips.title: der/die/das = er/sie/es
helpMemoryTips.text: In the nominative the article echoes the pronoun: der → **er**, die → **sie**, das → **es**.

helpMemoryTips.title: Endings beat meaning
helpMemoryTips.text: **das** Mädchen and **das** Kind are neuter because of the noun (-chen, das Kind), not the person. Grammar wins over logic.

helpMemoryTips.title: den for the masculi-n-e
helpMemoryTips.text: The extra **-n** marks the masculine accusative: de**n**, eine**n**, ih**n**, kei**n**en.

helpMemoryTips.title: Accusative pronouns

helpMemoryTips.title: See the contrast

en_de_m3_lesen.readingPassage: Mio ist ein kleines, grünes Monster mit einem riesigen Bauch, und Mio hat immer Hunger — wirklich immer! Heute beginnt das Chaos schon am Morgen. Zum Frühstück frisst Mio den Tisch, dann die Lampe und sogar das alte Sofa. „Mmh, lecker!", brummt es zufrieden. Zum Mittagessen nimmt Mio die Banane von Tom, den Stuhl aus der Küche und zum Nachtisch die Hausaufgaben — natürlich ohne ein einziges Wort der Entschuldigung. Da kommt Tom nach Hause und sieht das Monster mitten im Wohnzimmer. „Mio, nein! Nicht schon wieder!", ruft er verzweifelt. Aber Mio hört ihn überhaupt nicht. Es rülpst kurz, rennt durch den Garten, springt über den Zaun und sucht schon das nächste Haus. Die armen Nachbarn ahnen noch nichts von ihrem Glück.
en_de_m3_lesen.readingPassageTranslation: Mio is a small, green monster with a huge belly, and Mio is always hungry — really always! Today the chaos begins first thing in the morning. For breakfast Mio eats the table, then the lamp, and even the old sofa. "Mmh, yummy!" it growls contentedly. For lunch Mio takes Tom's banana, the chair from the kitchen, and for dessert the homework — without a single word of apology, of course. Then Tom comes home and sees the monster in the middle of the living room. "Mio, no! Not again!" he shouts in despair. But Mio doesn't hear him at all. It burps briefly, runs through the garden, jumps over the fence, and is already looking for the next house. The poor neighbours have no idea how lucky they've been so far.

en_de_m4_bigtext.readingPassage: Liebe Oma, was für ein wunderbares Fest! Du gibst wirklich immer allen etwas. Schon am Eingang drückst du dem Onkel ein dickes Buch in die Hand, der Tante schenkst du einen warmen Schal, und den Kindern gibst du so viel Schokolade, dass sie den ganzen Abend wild herumspringen. Der Onkel freut sich wie ein kleines Kind und liest sofort die erste Seite. In der Küche backst du auch noch den Kuchen ganz allein, und er schmeckt einfach allen am besten. Nach dem Essen setzen wir uns zusammen und spielen bis Mitternacht Karten. Am Ende umarme ich dich und danke dir von ganzem Herzen für diesen schönen Tag. Bleib gesund und bis ganz bald! Deine Anna
en_de_m4_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: Dear Oma, what a wonderful celebration! You really do always give everyone something. Right at the door you press a thick book into Uncle's hand, you give Aunt a warm scarf, and you give the children so much chocolate that they bounce around wildly all evening. Uncle is as happy as a little child and immediately reads the first page. In the kitchen you also bake the cake all by yourself, and it simply tastes the best to everyone. After the meal we sit down together and play cards until midnight. At the end I hug you and thank you from the bottom of my heart for this lovely day. Stay healthy and see you very soon! Your Anna

en_de_m5_bigtext.title: Big text: Ein Montagmorgen
en_de_m5_bigtext.helpMemoryIntro: Choose the case for each marked phrase — and for the last one, type the article. Watch the trick: "der Vater" (Wer? → Nominativ) vs "der Mutter" (Wem? → Dativ) — same word, different job.

helpMemoryTips.title: Three jobs, three questions
helpMemoryTips.text: **Wer?** → the doer → Nominativ. **Wen?/Was?** → the direct object → Akkusativ. **Wem?** → the receiver → Dativ.

helpMemoryTips.title: Wer – Wen – Wem
helpMemoryTips.text: The question word carries the case: We**r** (Nom), We**n** (Akk), We**m** (Dat) — same order as Nom → Akk → Dat.

helpMemoryTips.title: der masculine across the cases
helpMemoryTips.text: **der** Mann (Nom) → **den** Mann (Akk) → **dem** Mann (Dat). The masculine is where all three show up most clearly.

helpMemoryTips.title: Same word, different job
helpMemoryTips.text: **der** Vater (Wer? → Nom) vs **der** Mutter (Wem? → Dat): identical word "der", opposite case. Read the job, not the word.

en_de_m5_bigtext.readingPassage: Es ist wieder Montagmorgen, und im Haus von Familie Becker geht alles drunter und drüber. Lukas steht als Erster auf, noch halb im Schlaf. In der Küche macht er einen starken Kaffee für das Frühstück. Seine Schwester Mia schläft noch tief, deshalb bringt Lukas ihr den Kaffee direkt ans Bett. „Du bist der beste Bruder der Welt!", murmelt Mia verschlafen. Nach dem Frühstück gibt Mia dem Hund schnell sein Futter und vergisst dabei fast ihre Tasche. Der Hund heißt Bello und wedelt vor Freude mit dem ganzen Körper. en_de_m6_bigtext.title: Big text: Die Katze in der Stadt
en_de_m6_bigtext.helpMemoryIntro: For each marked phrase pick the case. Ask: is the cat moving there (Wohin? → Akkusativ) or already there (Wo? → Dativ)? Watch the pairs: sich setzen unter einen Tisch vs sitzen unter dem Tisch.

helpMemoryTips.title: The nine two-way prepositions
helpMemoryTips.text: **an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen** — accusative for motion (Wohin?), dative for position (Wo?).

helpMemoryTips.title: Wohin → Akk, Wo → Dat
helpMemoryTips.text: Moving to a *new* place = **Akkusativ** (into). Already *being* there = **Dativ** (in). Even "Wohi**n**" ends in -n, like de**n**.

helpMemoryTips.title: The classic pair
helpMemoryTips.text: Die Katze springt auf **den** Tisch (Wohin? → Akk) — und sitzt dann auf **dem** Tisch (Wo? → Dat).

helpMemoryTips.title: Let the verb decide
helpMemoryTips.text: Motion verbs (gehen, springen, legen, stellen, sich setzen) → **Akk**. Position verbs (sein, sitzen, liegen, stehen, bleiben) → **Dat**.

helpMemoryTips.title: Handy contractions
helpMemoryTips.text: in+das = **ins**, in+dem = **im**, an+das = **ans**, an+dem = **am**, auf+das = **aufs**.

en_de_m6_bigtext.readingPassage: Heute hat die kleine Katze Minka große Pläne: Sie geht ganz allein in die Stadt. Zuerst springt sie elegant auf eine Bank und beobachtet neugierig die vielen Menschen. Dann schleicht sie in ein gemütliches Café und setzt sich frech unter einen Tisch. Dort sitzt sie ganz ruhig unter dem Tisch und wartet auf einen Krümel Kuchen. Plötzlich stürmt ein großer, lauter Hund herein! Minka erschrickt, springt blitzschnell auf den Schrank und bleibt zitternd oben auf dem Schrank, bis der Hund endlich wieder draußen ist. Was für ein Abenteuer für so eine kleine Katze!

helpMemoryTips.title: The nine two-way prepositions
helpMemoryTips.text: **an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen** — accusative for motion (Wohin?), dative for position (Wo?).

helpMemoryTips.title: Wohin → Akk, Wo → Dat
helpMemoryTips.text: Moving to a *new* place = **Akkusativ** (into). Already *being* there = **Dativ** (in). Even "Wohi**n**" ends in -n, like de**n**.

helpMemoryTips.title: The classic pair
helpMemoryTips.text: Die Katze springt auf **den** Tisch (Wohin? → Akk) — und sitzt dann auf **dem** Tisch (Wo? → Dat).

helpMemoryTips.title: Let the verb decide
helpMemoryTips.text: Motion verbs (gehen, springen, legen, stellen, sich setzen) → **Akk**. Position verbs (sein, sitzen, liegen, stehen, bleiben) → **Dat**.

helpMemoryTips.title: Handy contractions
helpMemoryTips.text: in+das = **ins**, in+dem = **im**, an+das = **ans**, an+dem = **am**, auf+das = **aufs**.

en_de_m7_bigtext.title: Big text: Die neue Wohnung
en_de_m7_bigtext.helpMemoryIntro: Type the full adjective with its ending (the base form is the hint). Decide der-word vs ein-word and the case: eine neue Wohnung, das große Wohnzimmer, ein neues Sofa…

helpMemoryTips.title: Who already shows the gender?
helpMemoryTips.text: After **der/die/das** the article shows the case, so the adjective relaxes to weak **-e** (or **-en**). After **ein/kein/mein** the adjective must show it: **-er** (m), **-e** (f), **-es** (n).

helpMemoryTips.title: der → -e, ein → -er/-es
helpMemoryTips.text: *der nett**e** Mann* (der did the work) vs *ein nett**er** Mann* (ein hides the gender, so the adjective shows -er).

helpMemoryTips.title: After sein/werden/bleiben: nothing
helpMemoryTips.text: A predicate adjective never changes: Das Haus ist **alt**. Die Suppe wird **kalt**. Die Kinder bleiben **ruhig**.

helpMemoryTips.title: Nominative quick table
helpMemoryTips.text: der alt**e** Mann · die neu**e** Lampe · das klein**e** Kind — ein alt**er** Mann · eine neu**e** Lampe · ein klein**es** Kind.

en_de_m7_bigtext.readingPassage: Endlich, nach einer langen Suche, habe ich eine neue Wohnung gefunden — und ich bin überglücklich! Das große Wohnzimmer ist hell und super gemütlich; morgens scheint die Sonne direkt herein. In der Ecke steht ein neues Sofa, weich wie eine Wolke, und an der Wand hängt ein schönes Bild von einem alten Hafen. Die kleine Küche ist zwar nicht groß, aber modern und praktisch. Mein gemütliches Schlafzimmer hat ein riesiges Fenster mit Blick über die ganze Stadt. Nur einen Nachteil gibt es: Der Nachbar übt jeden Abend Trompete. Trotzdem — ich liebe meine neue Wohnung über alles!
en_de_m7_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: Finally, after a long search, I've found a new apartment — and I'm overjoyed! The living room is bright and super cosy; in the morning the sun shines straight in. In the corner there is a new sofa, soft as a cloud, and on the wall hangs a beautiful picture of an old harbour. The kitchen isn't big, but it's modern and practical. My bedroom has a huge window with a view over the whole city. There is only one drawback: the neighbour practises the trumpet every evening. Even so — I love my new apartment more than anything!

en_de_m8_bigtext.title: Big text: Mein chaotisches Wochenende
en_de_m8_bigtext.helpMemoryIntro: The full Perfekt: choose the helper (haben, or sein for movement — fahren, gehen, kommen) and form the participle. The helper sits in position 2, the participle jumps to the very end.

helpMemoryTips.title: haben/sein + participle
helpMemoryTips.text: Perfekt = **haben** or **sein** (position 2) + the past participle at the very end: Ich **habe** Fußball **gespielt**.

helpMemoryTips.title: Building participles
helpMemoryTips.text: Regular: **ge-** + stem + **-t** (ge·mach·t, ge·spiel·t). Strong: **ge-** + stem + **-en**, often with a vowel change (ge·gess·en, ge·trunk·en, ge·gang·en).

helpMemoryTips.title: sein = movement / change of state
helpMemoryTips.text: gehen → ist **gegangen**, fahren → ist **gefahren**, kommen → ist **gekommen**, bleiben → ist **geblieben**, sein → ist **gewesen**. Everything else takes **haben**.

helpMemoryTips.title: No ge- with -ieren / be-/ver-/er-
helpMemoryTips.text: Verbs in -ieren and inseparable be-/ver-/er- verbs drop ge-: studier**t**, telefonier**t**, **be**·such·t, **ver**·gess·en.

helpMemoryTips.title: Word order
helpMemoryTips.text: Gestern **habe** ich Pizza **gegessen.** — helper second, participle last.

Am Samstag bin ich durch die ganze Altstadt gegangen und habe dabei hundert Fotos gemacht. Abends habe ich in einem Biergarten ein riesiges Bier getrunken. Am Sonntag bin ich völlig erschöpft nach Hause gekommen. Mein Geld ist weg, aber die Erinnerungen bleiben!

On Saturday I walked through the whole old town and took a hundred photos. In the evening I drank a huge beer in a beer garden. On Sunday I came home completely exhausted. My money is gone, but the memories remain!

helpMemoryTips.title: Building participles
helpMemoryTips.text: Regular: **ge-** + stem + **-t** (ge·mach·t, ge·spiel·t). Strong: **ge-** + stem + **-en**, often with a vowel change (ge·gess·en, ge·trunk·en, ge·gang·en).

helpMemoryTips.title: sein = movement / change of state

en_de_m9_bigtext.title: Big text: Mein Tag
en_de_m9_bigtext.helpMemoryIntro: Type the missing verb form. For separable verbs type only the conjugated part (the prefix auf/an/fern is already in the sentence); for modals type the modal.

helpMemoryTips.title: The modal frame
helpMemoryTips.text: The modal is conjugated in position 2; the main verb waits at the end as an **infinitive**: Ich **kann** Deutsch **sprechen**.

helpMemoryTips.title: Modals: no -t for er
helpMemoryTips.text: The singular changes its vowel and ich = er: ich **kann**, du **kannst**, er **kann** · ich **muss**, er **muss** · ich **will**, er **will**.

helpMemoryTips.title: Separable verbs split
helpMemoryTips.text: The prefix flies to the end: auf·stehen → Ich stehe um 7 **auf**. ein·kaufen → Ich kaufe **ein**. an·rufen → Ich rufe dich **an**.

helpMemoryTips.title: Imperative drops the pronoun
helpMemoryTips.text: **Komm!** · **Wartet!** · **Öffnen Sie!** (du usually drops -st: du kommst → **Komm!**, but: du gibst → **Gib!**).

helpMemoryTips.title: The six modals
helpMemoryTips.text: **können, müssen, wollen, sollen, dürfen, mögen** — plus the polite **möchte** (would like).

en_de_m9_bigtext.readingPassage: Mein Montag ist immer randvoll! Um halb sieben klingelt der Wecker, und ich stehe sofort auf — na ja, fast sofort. Zuerst will ich unbedingt einen Kaffee trinken, sonst funktioniere ich einfach nicht. Auf dem Weg zur Arbeit rufe ich kurz meine Mutter an und frage, wie es ihr geht. Den ganzen Vormittag muss ich am Computer arbeiten, das ist manchmal ganz schön anstrengend. Am Nachmittag kann ich endlich Deutsch lernen — mein Lieblingsteil des Tages! Am Abend sehen wir alle zusammen fern und lachen über schlechte Serien. Um elf gehe ich todmüde ins Bett und schlafe sofort ein.
en_de_m9_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: My Monday is always jam-packed! At half past six the alarm rings, and I get up immediately — well, almost immediately. First I really want to drink a coffee, otherwise I simply don't function. On the way to work I quickly call my mother and ask how she is. All morning I have to work at the computer, which is sometimes pretty exhausting. In the afternoon I can finally study German — my favourite part of the day! In the evening we all watch TV together and laugh about bad series. At eleven I go to bed dead tired and fall asleep at once.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚑E8 Adjective AFTER the noun
helpMemoryTips.text: el coche rojo — the red car. Spanish puts most adjectives after the noun, the mirror of English.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚑E5 Accents are spelling
helpMemoryTips.text: está, cómo, adiós — the written accent is part of the word. Missing it is a spelling mistake, so type it.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚑E7 The article is part of the word
helpMemoryTips.text: Never learn "mesa" — learn "la mesa". The gender drives articles AND adjectives, so it must come bundled.

helpMemoryTips.title: The famous exceptions
helpMemoryTips.text: el día, el mapa, el problema (masculine despite -a); la mano (feminine despite -o). A short list — memorise it early.

en_es_a1_1_greetings.helpMemoryIntro: Your first Spanish words: greetings for every hour of the day.

helpMemoryTips.title: Buenos vs buenas
helpMemoryTips.text: buenos días (masculine plural) but buenas tardes / buenas noches (feminine plural) — your first taste of gender agreement (⚑E7).

helpMemoryTips.title: One form, all amounts
helpMemoryTips.text: Unlike is/are, hay is invariable: hay un libro, hay muchos libros. One worry fewer.

helpMemoryTips.title: Catch the key words
helpMemoryTips.text: Listen for de dónde (where from), años (age) and me gusta (likes). Three anchors answer everything.

en_es_a1_1_numbers.helpMemoryIntro: The numbers 0 to 20 — the building blocks of every price, age and phone number.

helpMemoryTips.text: Me llamo, se llama — literally "calls himself/herself". Spanish introduces names reflexively.

helpMemoryTips.title: The ser table
helpMemoryTips.text: yo soy · tú eres · él/ella/usted es · nosotros somos · ustedes/ellos son (Spain adds vosotros sois ⚑E28).

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚑E10 Drop the pronoun
helpMemoryTips.text: Soy médico already means "I am a doctor" — the -oy ending says who. Add yo only for emphasis.

en_es_a1_1_speak_intro.helpMemoryIntro: Introduce yourself in Spanish — listen and repeat.

en_es_a1_1_un_una.helpMemoryIntro: The indefinite article agrees too: un libro, una mesa. Plural unos/unas means "some".

helpMemoryTips.title: No article with professions
helpMemoryTips.text: The mirror image of English! Soy médico, es profesora — Spanish DROPS the article before professions (⚑E26).

en_es_a1_1_vowels.title: The five pure vowels

subjects.display: La niña pequeña habla español mañana.

en_es_a1_1_vowels.helpMemoryIntro: Spanish has exactly five vowel sounds — a e i o u — and they never change or reduce. Master these and your accent is halfway there.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚑E1 No schwa, ever
helpMemoryTips.text: English relaxes unstressed vowels ("banana" → buh-NAH-nuh). Spanish never does: ba-na-na, every a identical.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚑E2 The r is a tap
helpMemoryTips.text: pero has a single tap of the tongue, like the tt in American "butter". perro rolls it — two different words!

helpMemoryTips.title: The -ar endings
helpMemoryTips.text: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -an (Spain adds -áis ⚑E28). Learn them as a song: hablo-hablas-habla…

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚑E10 No pronoun needed
helpMemoryTips.text: Trabajo en Madrid = I work in Madrid. Adding yo is emphasis, not grammar.

helpMemoryTips.text: No preposition: el lunes trabajo = on Monday I work; los lunes = on Mondays. And days are NOT capitalised.

helpMemoryTips.title: Only nosotros differs
helpMemoryTips.text: comemos (-er) vs vivimos (-ir) — everywhere else the two families match. One table, two verbs.

en_es_a1_2_estar.title: estar: location and states

subjects.display: The keys are on the table.

Where are you? (tú) → ¿Dónde ____?

en_es_a1_2_estar.helpMemoryIntro: Spanish has TWO verbs "to be". estar = where things are and how they feel right now: estoy en casa, estoy cansado (⚑E11).

helpMemoryTips.title: The first rule of ser/estar
helpMemoryTips.text: WHERE and HOW-right-now → estar. WHO/WHAT something is → ser. Madrid está en España, pero Madrid es una ciudad.

en_es_a1_2_family.title: Family · La familia
en_es_a1_2_family.helpMemoryIntro: The close family. Note: padres = parents, parientes = relatives — the false friend cuts both ways (⚑E25).

helpMemoryTips.title: Masculine plural covers both
helpMemoryTips.text: los padres = mum and dad, los hermanos = brothers and sisters, los hijos = children. The masculine plural is the mixed-group default.

en_es_a1_2_gustar.helpMemoryIntro: gustar works backwards: Me gusta el café = coffee pleases me. Singular thing → gusta, plural things → gustan (⚑E12).

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚑E12 The verb agrees with the THING
helpMemoryTips.text: Me gusta el café (one thing) · Me gustan los libros (many things). Never "yo gusto café".

helpMemoryTips.title: Change the person, not the verb
helpMemoryTips.text: me/te/le/nos/les gusta(n): le gusta = he or she likes. The front pronoun carries who.

en_es_a1_2_listen_day.title: Listening: Un día normal
en_es_a1_2_listen_day.helpMemoryIntro: Lucía's routine. Listen for the times and the days.

helpMemoryTips.title: a las + hour
helpMemoryTips.text: se levanta a las seis, a las tres — "a las" flags every time of day. Use it as your anchor while listening.

en_es_a1_2_listen_day.readingPassage: Lucía trabaja en un hospital. Se levanta a las seis y desayuna un café con pan. Trabaja de siete a tres. Por la tarde estudia inglés y los martes nada en la piscina. Por la noche cena con su familia y lee un poco. Se acuesta a las once.
en_es_a1_2_listen_day.readingPassageTranslation: Lucía works in a hospital. She gets up at six and has coffee with bread for breakfast. She works from seven to three. In the afternoon she studies English, and on Tuesdays she swims in the pool. At night she has dinner with her family and reads a little. She goes to bed at eleven.

readingQuestions.question: ¿A qué hora se levanta Lucía?
readingQuestions.questionTranslation: What time does Lucía get up?

en_es_a1_2_read_week.title: Reading: La semana de Daniel
en_es_a1_2_read_week.helpMemoryIntro: Daniel's week. Notice the third-person endings and le gusta/le encantan.

helpMemoryTips.title: computadora vs ordenador
helpMemoryTips.text: Latin America says computadora, Spain says ordenador (⚑E28). Both are correct — recognise both.

en_es_a1_2_read_week.readingPassage: Daniel es de Toronto, pero vive en la Ciudad de México. Trabaja desde casa con su computadora. De lunes a viernes se levanta a las ocho, bebe un café grande y trabaja hasta las cinco. Le gusta mucho su trabajo. Los sábados va al mercado y compra fruta, pan y flores. Los domingos no trabaja: desayuna tarde, lee y llama a su familia en Canadá. Le encantan los domingos.
en_es_a1_2_read_week.readingPassageTranslation: Daniel is from Toronto, but he lives in Mexico City. He works from home on his computer. From Monday to Friday he gets up at eight, drinks a big coffee and works until five. He likes his job a lot. On Saturdays he goes to the market and buys fruit, bread and flowers. On Sundays he doesn't work: he has a late breakfast, reads and calls his family in Canada. He loves Sundays.

readingQuestions.question: ¿Qué compra los sábados?
readingQuestions.questionTranslation: What does he buy on Saturdays?

readingQuestions.question: ¿Qué hace los domingos?

readingQuestions.questionTranslation: What does he do on Sundays?

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚑E13 The little me/se
helpMemoryTips.text: me levanto, se ducha — routine verbs carry a reflexive pronoun. It is part of the verb: say it every time.

helpMemoryTips.title: tener expressions
helpMemoryTips.text: tener hambre (hungry), tener sed (thirsty), tener prisa (in a hurry), tener … años (age): Spanish HAS these states.

en_es_a2_1_bigtext.title: Big text: Un lunes extraño
en_es_a2_1_bigtext.helpMemoryIntro: Complete the story: preterite or imperfect in every gap.

helpMemoryTips.title: Paint or click?
helpMemoryTips.text: Read the whole story first. Then per gap: background painting → imperfect; plot advancing → preterite.

en_es_a2_1_bigtext.readingPassage: El lunes pasado fue un día extraño. Me levanté tarde porque el despertador no sonó. Cuando salí de casa, hacía mucho frío y la calle estaba vacía. Caminé al trabajo y llegué a las diez. La oficina estaba cerrada. Entonces vi un mensaje en la puerta: «Hoy es festivo». Yo no lo sabía. Así que volví a casa, me hice un café grande y vi películas todo el día. ¡Fue un lunes perfecto al final!
en_es_a2_1_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: Last Monday was a strange day. I got up late because the alarm didn't ring. When I left the house, it was very cold and the street was empty. I walked to work and arrived at ten. The office was closed. Then I saw a message on the door: "Today is a holiday." I didn't know. So I went back home, made myself a big coffee and watched films all day. It was a perfect Monday in the end!

en_es_a2_1_contrast.helpMemoryIntro: The heart of Spanish storytelling (⚑E14): imperfect paints the scene, preterite fires the events. English "was/used to" → imperfect; one-off done deals → preterite.

helpMemoryTips.title: Camera test
helpMemoryTips.text: Background video → imperfect (llovía, era tarde). Snapshot click → preterite (entró, llamó, vi).

helpMemoryTips.title: Only three irregulars
helpMemoryTips.text: ser→era, ir→iba, ver→veía. Everything else is regular — the friendliest tense in Spanish.

helpMemoryTips.text: ir/ser→fui · tener→tuve · hacer→hice · estar→estuve · poder→pude · decir→dije · ver→vi · dar→di.

en_es_a2_1_listen_trip.readingPassage: El mes pasado Daniel y yo fuimos a Oaxaca en autobús. El viaje duró seis horas, pero el paisaje era precioso. El sábado visitamos el mercado y comimos tlayudas. helpMemoryTips.title: hablo vs habló
helpMemoryTips.text: The accent IS the tense: hablo = I speak, habló = he spoke. Type the accent or change the meaning.

en_es_a2_1_read_childhood.title: Reading: La infancia de doña Rosa
en_es_a2_1_read_childhood.helpMemoryIntro: A short biography. Watch the two pasts at work: tenía, era, había paint; nació, se mudó, conoció click.

helpMemoryTips.title: conocer in the preterite = met
helpMemoryTips.text: conocía = knew · conoció = met (first time). Some verbs change meaning between the two pasts — collect them.

en_es_a2_1_read_childhood.readingPassage: Doña Rosa nació en un pueblo pequeño cerca de Valencia. Su familia tenía una huerta con naranjos. Cuando era niña, se levantaba a las seis y ayudaba a su padre antes de ir a la escuela. No había televisión, así que por las noches su abuela contaba historias. A los dieciocho años, doña Rosa se mudó a la ciudad y encontró trabajo en una panadería. Allí conoció a su marido. «Fueron años difíciles», dice, «pero también los más felices de mi vida».
en_es_a2_1_read_childhood.readingPassageTranslation: Doña Rosa was born in a small village near Valencia. Her family had an orchard with orange trees. When she was a girl, she got up at six and helped her father before going to school. There was no television, so at night her grandmother told stories. At eighteen, doña Rosa moved to the city and found work in a bakery. There she met her husband. "They were hard years," she says, "but also the happiest of my life."

readingQuestions.question: ¿Dónde nació doña Rosa?

helpMemoryTips.text: Every gap is a module rock: check whether the object is a person (→ a) and where the pronoun goes.

en_es_a2_2_bigtext.readingPassage: Este sábado voy a hacer muchas cosas. Por la mañana tengo que limpiar el apartamento. Después voy a visitar a mi abuela — la llamo todos los días, pero quiero verla en persona. Vamos a comer en su restaurante favorito, que es más barato que el centro. en_es_a2_2_read_market.readingPassage: Los sábados por la mañana, Emma va al mercado de su barrio en Valencia. Es más barato que el supermercado y la fruta es mejor. Primero compra naranjas y tomates; el vendedor, don Paco, siempre le da una mandarina gratis. Después busca a su amiga Carmen, que vende flores en la esquina. «¿Vas a venir a la cena del domingo?», le pregunta Carmen. «¡Claro! Voy a llevar una tortilla», responde Emma. Tiene que practicar: la primera vez la cocinó demasiado. Esta semana va a comprar más huevos, por si acaso.
en_es_a2_2_read_market.readingPassageTranslation: On Saturday mornings, Emma goes to her neighbourhood market in Valencia. It is cheaper than the supermarket and the fruit is better. First she buys oranges and tomatoes; the seller, don Paco, always gives her a free tangerine. Then she looks for her friend Carmen, who sells flowers on the corner. "Are you going to come to Sunday's dinner?" Carmen asks her. "Of course! I'm going to bring a tortilla," Emma replies. She has to practise: the first time she overcooked it. This week she is going to buy extra eggs, just in case.

en_es_b1_1_bigtext.readingPassage: Emma, quiero que me escuches bien: la paella no se hace con prisa. Primero, es importante que el arroz sea bueno. Pon el fuego lento y no lo toques tanto — ¡no seas impaciente! Mi madre siempre decía: «Ten paciencia, hija». No creo que la primera te salga perfecta, pero espero que lo intentes otra vez. Yo sé hacer paella desde los quince años, y todavía aprendo. Este azafrán es para ti — lo compré por muy poco dinero en el mercado. ¡Suerte!
en_es_b1_1_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: Emma, I want you to listen to me carefully: paella is not made in a hurry. First, it is important that the rice is good. Put the heat on low and don't touch it so much — don't be impatient! My mother always said: "Have patience, my girl." I don't think your first one will come out perfect, but I hope you try again. I have known how to make paella since I was fifteen, and I am still learning. This saffron is for you — I bought it for very little money at the market. Good luck!

en_es_b1_1_read_letter.title: Reading: La carta de la abuela
en_es_b1_1_read_letter.helpMemoryIntro: A grandmother's letter, stitched together with subjunctives, commands and one saber/conocer pair.

helpMemoryTips.title: Feelings breed subjunctive
helpMemoryTips.text: me alegra que estés, quiere que comas, espero que seas — every emotion pulls the next verb into the subjunctive.

en_es_b1_1_read_letter.readingPassage: Querido Daniel: Me alegra mucho que estés contento en México y que tu español mejore cada semana. Tu madre quiere que comas mejor — ¡no vivas solo de tacos! Yo solo espero que seas feliz. Te recomiendo que conozcas Oaxaca; tu abuelo y yo la visitamos hace cuarenta años y nunca la olvidamos. Cuando vengas en diciembre, haz una lista de todo lo que quieres contarme. Y no esperes tanto para escribir: sabes que tus cartas son mi alegría. Un abrazo enorme, tu abuela Rose.
en_es_b1_1_read_letter.readingPassageTranslation: Dear Daniel: I am so glad that you are happy in Mexico and that your Spanish improves every week. Your mother wants you to eat better — don't live on tacos alone! I only hope you are happy. I recommend that you get to know Oaxaca; your grandfather and I visited it forty years ago and never forgot it. When you come in December, make a list of everything you want to tell me. And don't wait so long to write: you know your letters are my joy. A huge hug, your grandmother Rose.

readingQuestions.question: ¿Cuándo va a venir Daniel?
readingQuestions.questionTranslation: When is Daniel going to come?

helpMemoryTips.text: First pass: understand the story. Second pass: paint (imperfect), click (preterite), and one step back (había).

en_es_b1_2_bigtext.readingPassage: Era una noche de viento y yo veía una película antigua en casa. De repente se apagaron las luces. Mientras buscaba una vela, alguien llamó a la puerta. Era mi vecina, la señora Vega, que antes era electricista. «¿Tienes una linterna? Préstamela y te lo arreglo», dijo. Se la presté y en diez minutos volvió la luz. Resulta que un cable viejo se había roto. «Si mañana no hay luz otra vez», me dijo, «llámame y te la ayudo». Por suerte, no fue necesario. ¡Qué vecina!
en_es_b1_2_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: It was a windy night and I was watching an old film at home. Suddenly the lights went out. While I was looking for a candle, someone knocked at the door. It was my neighbour, señora Vega, who used to be an electrician. "Do you have a torch? Lend it to me and I'll fix it for you," she said. I lent it to her and in ten minutes the light came back. It turns out an old cable had broken. "If there's no light again tomorrow," she told me, "call me and I'll help you." Luckily, it wasn't necessary. What a neighbour!

en_es_b1_2_listen_anecdote.title: Listening: La llave perdida
en_es_b1_2_listen_anecdote.helpMemoryIntro: A full anecdote: two pasts, a past perfect, a no-fault se and the connectors in action.

helpMemoryTips.title: se me había caído
helpMemoryTips.text: The no-fault se meets the past perfect: "it had fallen from me". Spanish stacks its machinery neatly — listen for it.

en_es_b1_2_listen_anecdote.readingPassage: El viernes pasado me pasó algo increíble. Volvía a casa cansado y, cuando busqué la llave, no estaba. Se me había caído en algún sitio. Llamé a mi compañera de piso, pero no contestó. Así que me senté a esperar en la escalera. Entonces la vecina abrió su puerta y me dijo: «¿Buscas esto? La encontré en el ascensor esta mañana». ¡Había llevado mi llave en el bolsillo todo el día! Por suerte, todo acabó bien. Ahora siempre la guardo en el mismo bolsillo.
en_es_b1_2_listen_anecdote.readingPassageTranslation: Last Friday something incredible happened to me. I was coming home tired and, when I looked for my key, it wasn't there. I had dropped it somewhere. I called my flatmate, but she didn't answer. So I sat down to wait on the stairs. Then the neighbour opened her door and said: "Looking for this? I found it in the lift this morning." She had carried my key in her pocket all day! Luckily, everything ended well. Now I always keep it in the same pocket.

readingQuestions.question: ¿Qué había pasado con la llave?
readingQuestions.questionTranslation: What had happened to the key?

en_es_b1_2_read_story.title: Reading: La maleta equivocada
en_es_b1_2_read_story.helpMemoryIntro: A travel mix-up with past perfects, se lo pronouns and a peek at the B2 conditional.

helpMemoryTips.title: resulta que…
helpMemoryTips.text: "It turns out that…" — the connector every Spanish storyteller leans on for the twist. Steal it.

en_es_b1_2_read_story.readingPassage: Cuando Daniel llegó al hotel de Lima, abrió la maleta y se quedó helado: dentro había vestidos, zapatos de tacón y un sombrero rojo. ¡Se había llevado la maleta equivocada! En el aeropuerto, una mujer con una maleta idéntica había recogido la suya. Por suerte, dentro del sombrero había una tarjeta con un teléfono. La llamó y resulta que la mujer, una cantante de tango argentina, estaba en el mismo barrio. Se encontraron en un café, intercambiaron las maletas y ella le regaló dos entradas para su concierto. «Si no te hubieras equivocado de maleta», le dijo riendo, «nunca habrías escuchado tango en vivo». Y tenía razón: fue la mejor noche del viaje.
en_es_b1_2_read_story.readingPassageTranslation: When Daniel arrived at his hotel in Lima, he opened the suitcase and froze: inside there were dresses, high-heeled shoes and a red hat. He had taken the wrong suitcase! At the airport, a woman with an identical case had picked up his. Luckily, inside the hat there was a card with a phone number. He called it, and it turns out the woman, an Argentinian tango singer, was in the same neighbourhood. They met in a café, exchanged suitcases and she gave him two tickets to her concert. "If you hadn't taken the wrong suitcase," she said, laughing, "you would never have heard live tango." And she was right: it was the best night of the trip.

readingQuestions.question: ¿Qué había dentro de la maleta?

en_es_b2_1_bigtext.title: Big text: La ciudad ideal

en_es_b2_1_bigtext.readingPassage: ¿Cómo sería mi ciudad ideal? Si yo fuera alcaldesa, lo primero que haría sería plantar mil árboles. Habría menos coches y más tranvías, y los niños, cuyos parques hoy están llenos de tráfico, podrían jugar en la calle. Si los alquileres no fueran tan caros, los jóvenes no se irían. Habría que invertir mucho dinero, es verdad; sin embargo, lo que hoy parece caro mañana sería barato. A lo mejor nunca seré alcaldesa. Pero si algún día me dieran el puesto, ya tengo el plan.
en_es_b2_1_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: What would my ideal city be like? If I were mayor, the first thing I would do would be to plant a thousand trees. There would be fewer cars and more trams, and the children, whose parks today are full of traffic, could play in the street. If rents weren't so expensive, young people wouldn't leave. A lot of money would have to be invested, it's true; however, what seems expensive today would be cheap tomorrow. Maybe I'll never be mayor. But if one day they gave me the job, I already have the plan.

en_es_b2_1_listen_debate.readingPassage: Esta noche, en el programa: ¿debería nuestra ciudad construir un tranvía? «Si tuviéramos tranvía, habría menos coches en el centro», dice la concejala Ruiz. «Lo que necesitamos no es un tranvía carísimo, sino más autobuses», responde el señor Ortega, cuyo barrio quedaría fuera de la línea. «Las obras durarían tres años y los comercios sufrirían». La concejala admite que las obras serían molestas, pero insiste: «Si no invirtiéramos ahora, lo pagaríamos durante décadas». El debate continúa la próxima semana.
en_es_b2_1_listen_debate.readingPassageTranslation: Tonight on the programme: should our city build a tram? "If we had a tram, there would be fewer cars in the centre," says councillor Ruiz. "What we need is not a hugely expensive tram but more buses," replies Mr. Ortega, whose neighbourhood would be left off the line. "The works would take three years and local shops would suffer." The councillor admits the works would be annoying, but insists: "If we didn't invest now, we would pay for it for decades." The debate continues next week.

en_es_b2_1_read_essay.title: Reading: ¿Y si trabajáramos menos?
en_es_b2_1_read_essay.helpMemoryIntro: An opinion piece powered by conditionals, lo que and cuyo — the B2 argument in written form.

helpMemoryTips.title: Concede, then turn
helpMemoryTips.text: Sin embargo, no todo sería tan sencillo — the concession pivot. Every good argument has one; steal this one.

en_es_b2_1_read_essay.readingPassage: ¿Qué pasaría si la semana laboral tuviera cuatro días? Quienes defienden la idea dicen que produciríamos lo mismo en menos horas: descansados, cometeríamos menos errores y las empresas gastarían menos en oficinas. Lo que muestran los estudios piloto es prometedor: en las empresas que probaron el modelo, la productividad no bajó y los empleados, cuyos niveles de estrés se midieron durante un año, dormían mejor y se enfermaban menos. Sin embargo, no todo sería tan sencillo. Si un hospital redujera sus horas, ¿quién atendería a los pacientes del viernes? Habría que contratar más personal, y eso costaría dinero. A lo mejor la respuesta no es la misma para todos los sectores. Lo que parece claro es que la pregunta ya no es ridícula.
en_es_b2_1_read_essay.readingPassageTranslation: What would happen if the working week had four days? Those who defend the idea say we would produce the same in fewer hours: rested, we would make fewer mistakes and companies would spend less on offices. What the pilot studies show is promising: in the companies that tried the model, productivity didn't fall, and employees, whose stress levels were measured for a year, slept better and got ill less. However, not everything would be so simple. If a hospital reduced its hours, who would look after Friday's patients? More staff would have to be hired, and that would cost money. Maybe the answer is not the same for every sector. What seems clear is that the question is no longer ridiculous.

options: Quién atendería a los pacientes del viernes

en_es_b2_2_bigtext.readingPassage: El lunes Emma le dijo a su equipo que la clienta quería cambios. Tom entendió que la clienta estaba descontenta y le dijo a Daniel que tendrían que rehacer el diseño. Daniel dijo que era imposible: no había tiempo. «Hablaste tú misma con ella, ¿no?», preguntó. «Pues no. Su asistente me dijo que la clienta había visto los borradores», admitió Emma. «Estaría ocupada, como siempre». Al final, resulta que a la clienta le encantaba el diseño y solo había pedido que cambiaran un color. «La próxima vez», suspiró Daniel, «cuando alguien os mande un mensaje confuso, preguntad — aunque que parezca una tontería. Lo que hoy es un comentario, mañana será una crisis».
en_es_b2_2_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: On Monday Emma told her team that the client wanted changes. Tom understood the client was unhappy and told Daniel they would have to redo the design. Daniel said it was impossible: there was no time. "You spoke to her yourself, right?" he asked. "Well, no. Her assistant told me the client had seen the drafts," Emma admitted. "She was probably busy, as always." In the end, it turns out the client loved the design and had only asked them to change one colour. "Next time," Daniel sighed, "when someone sends you a confusing message, ask — even if it seems silly. What is a comment today will be a crisis tomorrow."

en_es_b2_2_read_email.readingPassage: El viernes, el jefe de Mateo le dijo que la fecha de entrega se había movido. Mateo entendió que tendría una semana más, así que dejó las pruebas finales para el lunes y pasó el fin de semana descansando. El lunes, su compañera le preguntó si había enviado el informe. «Sabías que la fecha era hoy, ¿no?», le dijo. Resulta que «adelantar» y «aplazar» no son lo mismo. Mateo se dio cuenta de su error demasiado tarde y le pidió al jefe que le diera un día más. «Te lo doy», respondió el jefe, «pero la próxima vez, cuando algo no esté claro, pregunta». Actualmente, Mateo tiene una regla de oro: si un mensaje puede entenderse de dos maneras, pregunta — aunque parezca una pregunta tonta.
en_es_b2_2_read_email.readingPassageTranslation: On Friday, Mateo's boss told him the deadline had been moved. Mateo understood he would have one more week, so he left the final tests for Monday and spent the weekend resting. On Monday, his colleague asked him if he had sent the report. "You knew the deadline was today, right?" she said. It turns out that "to move up" and "to postpone" are not the same thing. Mateo realised his mistake too late and asked his boss to give him one more day. "You've got it," the boss replied, "but next time, when something isn't clear, ask." Currently, Mateo has a golden rule: if a message can be understood two ways, ask — even if it seems a silly question.

Si el equipo hubiera recibido los materiales a tiempo, los resultados habrían sido otros. Por mucho que se invierta en marketing, sin distribución no hay ventas. Se ha llegado a un acuerdo con dos nuevos socios, y es posible que la situación haya mejorado ya en junio. A pesar de todo, el equipo ha hecho un gran esfuerzo. Digan lo que digan, la recuperación está en marcha.

An agreement has been reached with two new partners, and it is possible that the situation has already improved by June. In spite of everything, the team has made a great effort. en_es_c1_1_listen_lecture.title: Listening: La conferencia
en_es_c1_1_listen_lecture.helpMemoryIntro: A mini-lecture: concessives, lo + adjective and collocations in spoken academic Spanish.

helpMemoryTips.title: Listen for the scaffolding
helpMemoryTips.text: Primero… Segundo… Tercero, y quizá sea lo más importante… — the numbered skeleton is your map of any academic audio.

en_es_c1_1_listen_lecture.readingPassage: ¿Por qué crecen unas ciudades mientras otras se vacían? En términos generales, los investigadores señalan tres factores. Primero, el empleo: la gente sigue al trabajo, y las empresas siguen al talento — un círculo del que es difícil salir. Segundo, las universidades desempeñan un papel mayor de lo que se creía: los graduados suelen quedarse donde estudiaron. Tercero, y quizá sea lo más importante, la vivienda. Por mucho que crezca el empleo, si no se construyen casas, el crecimiento se va a otra parte. Lo curioso es que los precios altos expulsan precisamente a las empresas que iniciaron el círculo.
en_es_c1_1_listen_lecture.readingPassageTranslation: Why do some cities grow while others empty out? Broadly speaking, researchers point to three factors. First, employment: people follow work, and companies follow talent — a circle that is hard to leave. Second, universities play a bigger role than was believed: graduates tend to stay where they studied. Third, and perhaps most importantly, housing. However much employment grows, if houses are not built, the growth goes elsewhere. The curious thing is that high prices expel precisely the companies that started the circle.

en_es_c1_1_read_essay.title: Reading: La paradoja de elegir
en_es_c1_1_read_essay.helpMemoryIntro: A mini-essay with the module's full machinery: impersonal se, lo + adjective, concessives and hedged claims.

helpMemoryTips.title: No se trata de que…
helpMemoryTips.text: "It is not that…" + subjunctive — an elegant way to head off a misreading before it happens. Steal it for essays.

en_es_c1_1_read_essay.readingPassage: Se suele suponer que cuantas más opciones tenemos, más felices somos. La evidencia, sin embargo, apunta en otra dirección. En un estudio célebre, los clientes a quienes se ofrecieron veinticuatro variedades de mermelada compraron mucho menos que aquellos a quienes se ofrecieron solo seis. Lo paradójico es que el aumento de opciones parece elevar el coste de cada decisión: con tantas alternativas, el miedo a equivocarse pesa más que el placer de elegir. No se trata de que la variedad sea indeseable — se trata de que sus beneficios se estancan sorprendentemente pronto. Por muchas mermeladas que añadamos al estante, la número veinticuatro rara vez hace más feliz a nadie.
en_es_c1_1_read_essay.readingPassageTranslation: It is usually assumed that the more options we have, the happier we are. The evidence, however, points in another direction. In a famous study, customers who were offered twenty-four varieties of jam bought far less than those offered only six. The paradoxical thing is that the increase in options seems to raise the cost of every decision: with so many alternatives, the fear of choosing wrongly weighs more than the pleasure of choosing. It is not that variety is undesirable — it is that its benefits flatten out surprisingly early. However many jams we add to the shelf, jam number twenty-four rarely makes anyone happier.

readingQuestions.question: ¿Qué parece elevar el aumento de opciones?
readingQuestions.questionTranslation: What does the increase in options seem to raise?

readingQuestions.question: ¿Piensa el autor que la variedad es indeseable?
options: No — solo que sus beneficios se estancan pronto
readingQuestions.questionTranslation: Does the author think variety is undesirable?

helpMemoryTips.text: Every gap asks for the formal option: solicitar not pedir; realicen not hagan.

en_es_c1_2_bigtext.readingPassage: Estimada Sra. Serrano: Me dirijo a usted en relación con los retrasos que afectan a la línea 4. Si bien el servicio ha mejorado desde marzo, la situación actual sigue siendo inaceptable. Los trenes se cancelan sin previo aviso; es decir, los pasajeros rara vez reciben información sobre alternativas. Fue por otra pasajera como me enteré del cambio de horarios. Me veo obligada a solicitar que se publique un horario revisado y que se realicen los reembolsos correspondientes a los abonados. Le agradecería que estudiara además la frecuencia de los fines de semana. Dicho esto, quiero reconocer la amabilidad del personal. Lo que los pasajeros necesitan, en definitiva, es fiabilidad, no disculpas. Quedo a la espera de su respuesta. No dude en contactarme. Atentamente, M. Duarte.
en_es_c1_2_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: Dear Ms. Serrano: I am writing to you regarding the delays affecting Line 4. While the service has improved since March, the current situation remains unacceptable. Trains are cancelled without notice; that is to say, passengers rarely receive information about alternatives. It was through another passenger that I learned of the timetable change. I am obliged to request that a revised timetable be published and that the corresponding refunds be issued to season-ticket holders. I would also be grateful if you considered the weekend frequency. That said, I want to acknowledge the kindness of the staff. What passengers need, ultimately, is reliability, not apologies. I await your reply. Do not hesitate to contact me. Yours sincerely, M. Duarte.

en_es_c1_2_listen_panel.readingPassage: ¿Deberían ser gratuitos los museos? Si bien la entrada gratuita suena generosa, alguien paga siempre. Lo que hacen los museos gratuitos, en realidad, es trasladar el coste del turista al contribuyente. Dicho esto, la evidencia de Londres es llamativa: tras eliminarse las entradas en 2001, las visitas se triplicaron, y fueron las familias jóvenes, no los turistas, quienes impulsaron el aumento. Es decir, la cuestión no es si pagamos, sino qué decidimos pagar. En definitiva, un museo que nadie visita es el museo más caro de todos.
en_es_c1_2_listen_panel.readingPassageTranslation: Should museums be free? While free entry sounds generous, somebody always pays. What free museums actually do is shift the cost from the tourist to the taxpayer. That said, the evidence from London is striking: after fees were removed in 2001, visits tripled, and it was young families, not tourists, who drove the increase. In other words, the question is not whether we pay, but what we choose to pay for. Ultimately, a museum nobody visits is the most expensive museum of all.

helpMemoryTips.title: Steal the formal moulds
helpMemoryTips.text: Me dirijo a usted en relación con… / Me veo obligada a solicitar que… — two moulds that serve every formal complaint of your real life.

en_es_c1_2_read_letters.readingPassage: Versión uno, a una amiga: «¿Sabes qué? ¡El piso de arriba se inundó OTRA VEZ y mi techo está hecho un desastre! Le he pedido al casero mil veces que lo arregle. ¡Qué rabia!» Versión dos, al casero: «Estimado Sr. Vidal: Me dirijo a usted en relación con los daños causados en el techo de mi vivienda el 12 de marzo, a raíz de una inundación en el piso superior. Habiendo comunicado esta incidencia en cinco ocasiones anteriores, me veo obligada a solicitar que las reparaciones se realicen en un plazo de catorce días. De no atenderse la solicitud, me veré en la necesidad de contactar con la oficina municipal de vivienda. Atentamente, L. Ortiz.» El mismo techo, la misma agua — otro idioma.
en_es_c1_2_read_letters.readingPassageTranslation: Version one, to a friend: "You know what? The flat upstairs flooded AGAIN and my ceiling is a disaster! I've asked the landlord a thousand times to fix it. So annoying!" Version two, to the landlord: "Dear Mr. Vidal: I am writing to you regarding the damage caused to the ceiling of my home on 12 March, following a flood in the flat above. Having reported this issue on five previous occasions, I am obliged to request that the repairs be carried out within fourteen days. Should this request not be attended to, I will find it necessary to contact the municipal housing office. Yours sincerely, L. Ortiz." The same ceiling, the same water — another language.

en_es_c2_1_bigtext.title: Big text: La reseña
en_es_c2_1_bigtext.helpMemoryIntro: Complete an ironic restaurant review: idioms, diminutives and mood-meaning contrasts.

helpMemoryTips.title: Read the tone first
helpMemoryTips.text: The review praises with the brakes on and criticises smiling. Each gap keeps that temperature.

en_es_c2_1_bigtext.readingPassage: El Tenedor de Oro no es precisamente barato — la cena costó un ojo de la cara — pero se come de maravilla. Su famoso pastel de pescado quizá sea el mejor de la ciudad, aunque el camarero que lo describió durante seis minutos no fue, digamos, breve. El servicio es otra historia: los entrantes llegaron antes que la carta y el vino no llegó nunca. «Se me olvidó por completo», admitió el camarero, lo cual tuvo al menos el encanto de la honestidad. ¿Volvería? Creo que sí. No hay chef en el barrio que haga el hojaldre como este. Eso sí: la próxima vez pediré el vino en cuanto me siente, y no esperaré a que el camarero dé en el clavo con la carta. Al fin y al cabo, se perdona mucho por un postre así. Un consejo: reserven una mesita tranquila y pidan el pastel sin miedo. Más vale tarde que nunca.
en_es_c2_1_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: The Golden Fork is not exactly cheap — dinner cost an arm and a leg — but the food is wonderful. Its famous fish pie may well be the best in the city, although the waiter who described it for six minutes was not, shall we say, brief. The service is another story: the starters arrived before the menu and the wine never arrived at all. "It completely slipped my mind," the waiter admitted, which at least had the charm of honesty. Would I go back? I think so. There is no chef in the neighbourhood who does pastry like this one. Mind you: next time I'll order the wine as soon as they seat me, and I won't wait for the waiter to hit the nail on the head with the menu. At the end of the day, one forgives a great deal for a dessert like that. A tip: book a quiet little table and order the pie without fear. Better late than never.

en_es_c2_1_listen_sobremesa.title: Listening: La sobremesa
en_es_c2_1_listen_sobremesa.helpMemoryIntro: An after-lunch conversation full of diminutives, irony and cultural music. Listen for what is said between the lines.

helpMemoryTips.title: cuatro cositas
helpMemoryTips.text: When a Spanish host says "just a few little things", multiply by five. The diminutive is modesty theatre.

en_es_c2_1_listen_sobremesa.readingPassage: ¡Qué comidita, doña Rosa! — Nada, cuatro cositas… — ¿Cuatro? Llevamos tres horas en la mesa. — Eso es la sobremesa, hijo. Aquí no se come: se conversa con cuchara. — Pues en mi país, terminas el café y te vas. — ¡Qué horror! Ni se te ocurra hacer eso aquí. La última vez que un invitado se fue pronto, mi madre estuvo una semana preguntando si le había pasado algo. — Ya, claro, y ahora me toca quedarme hasta las siete. — Hasta las ocho, mínimo. Hay tarta. — Menudo sacrificio. — Oye, que la tarta la hice yo. — …¿Y si empezamos ahorita?
en_es_c2_1_listen_sobremesa.readingPassageTranslation: What a lovely meal, doña Rosa! — Oh, nothing, just a few little things… — A few? We've been at the table for three hours. — That's the sobremesa, dear. Here one doesn't eat: one converses with a spoon. — Well, in my country, you finish your coffee and leave. — How awful! Don't even think of doing that here. The last time a guest left early, my mother spent a week asking if something had happened to him. — Sure, of course, and now I have to stay until seven. — Until eight, minimum. There's cake. — What a sacrifice. — Hey, I made that cake myself. — …Shall we start right now-ish?

helpMemoryTips.text: Indicative points at something that exists and you know; subjunctive at something desired or unverified. The verb form IS the information.

en_es_c2_1_read_column.title: Reading: El columnista
en_es_c2_1_read_column.helpMemoryIntro: A humour column about the sobremesa: irony, rhythm and one affectionate diminutive as the punchline.

helpMemoryTips.title: Structural irony
helpMemoryTips.text: The column presents silence as maximum condemnation: the irony lives in the contrast, not in any single word.

en_es_c2_1_read_column.readingTitle: Sobre el arte de la sobremesa
en_es_c2_1_read_column.readingPassage: La sobremesa no es, como imaginan algunos visitantes, el rato perezoso que sigue al postre. Es una institución nacional. Levantarse de la mesa al terminar el café no es irse: es desertar. Que nadie diga nada no significa que no haya pasado nada — precisamente porque nadie dice nada, sabrás que has cometido un crimen. Un «¿ya te vas?» murmurado desde la cabecera equivale, en términos de sobremesa, a un motín. No somos, todo hay que decirlo, un pueblo dado a la prisa. Preferimos discutir de política, de fútbol y de si la tarta lleva demasiado azúcar, todo a la vez y durante tres horas. A los amigos extranjeros esto puede parecerles agotador. Lo es. Pero en la sobremesa, todo español, sea cual sea su partido, permanece unido: sentado, discutiendo, y pidiendo, por supuesto, otro cafecito.
en_es_c2_1_read_column.readingPassageTranslation: The sobremesa is not, as some visitors imagine, the lazy stretch after dessert. It is a national institution. Getting up from the table when the coffee ends is not leaving: it is deserting. That nobody says anything does not mean nothing has happened — precisely because nobody says anything, you will know you have committed a crime. A murmured "leaving already?" from the head of the table amounts, in sobremesa terms, to a mutiny. We are not, it must be said, a people given to hurry. We prefer to argue about politics, football and whether the cake has too much sugar, all at once and for three hours. To foreign friends this may seem exhausting. It is. But at the sobremesa, every Spaniard, whatever their party, stands united: seated, arguing, and ordering, of course, another cafecito.

readingQuestions.question: Según el texto, ¿qué es levantarse al terminar el café?
readingQuestions.questionTranslation: According to the text, what is getting up when the coffee ends?

readingQuestions.question: ¿Qué tono usa el columnista?
readingQuestions.questionTranslation: What tone does the columnist use?

en_es_c2_1_speaking_close.title: Final conversation: humour and nuance

helpMemoryTips.title: Undersell the drama

en_es_c2_2_bigtext.title: Big text: El discurso de graduación
en_es_c2_2_bigtext.helpMemoryIntro: The last gapped text: rhetoric, mood, register and the final traps — the whole course on one page.

helpMemoryTips.title: Course closer
helpMemoryTips.text: Every gap is a module you already own. Read it whole, enjoy it, and finish.

en_es_c2_2_bigtext.readingPassage: Amigos: nos reunimos para celebrar no un final, sino un comienzo. Nunca ha reunido esta sala tanto conocimiento ganado a pulso. Llegasteis sin poder pedir un café; os vais sabiendo discutir, bromear y cambiar de registro como quien se cambia de zapatos. La vida es corta y la gente es generosa con su paciencia: hablad, y hablad mal cuando haga falta, porque fueron los errores los que más os enseñaron. Por lejos que hayáis llegado, os preguntaréis qué viene ahora. Dicho de otro modo: todo. Al final, todo estudiante se da cuenta del secreto: nadie está terminado. Ni los profesores, ni los nativos, ni siquiera los poetas. Lo que llamamos maestría es simplemente curiosidad que no se rindió. Si alguien os dice que ya no queda nada por aprender, no le hagáis caso. Y cuando dudéis, recordad esta sala: digan lo que digan, el idioma ya es vuestro. Enhorabuena — ahora salid a usarlo.
en_es_c2_2_bigtext.readingPassageTranslation: Friends: we gather to celebrate not an ending but a beginning. Never has this room held so much hard-won knowledge. You arrived unable to order a coffee; you leave able to argue, to joke, to switch registers like someone changing shoes. Life is short and people are generous with their patience: speak, and speak badly when you must, because it was the mistakes that taught you the most. However far you have come, you will wonder what comes next. In other words: everything. In the end, every learner realises the secret: nobody is finished. Not the teachers, not the natives, not even the poets. What we call mastery is simply curiosity that did not give up. If anyone tells you there is nothing left to learn, pay them no attention. And when you doubt, remember this room: whatever they say, the language is already yours. Congratulations — now go out and use it.

helpMemoryTips.text: harina/recuerdos/ninguna idea · paciencia/preguntas/clientes: the speech is built in threes. Hear them land.

en_es_c2_2_listen_speech.readingPassage: Vecinos, amigos, alborotadores — ya saben quiénes son. Hace veinte años abrí esta panadería con un saco de harina y ninguna idea de lo que hacía. Hoy la dejo sin harina, con miles de recuerdos y, si soy sincera, con la misma ninguna idea. Este barrio me dio tres cosas: una paciencia que no tenía, preguntas que no sabía responder y clientes que, al final, las respondieron solos. Ese es el secreto que nadie cuenta: uno no vende pan. Uno presta confianza hasta que la gente se da cuenta — y vaya si se da cuenta — de que siempre fue suya. Gracias, y cuidado con el escalón al salir.
en_es_c2_2_listen_speech.readingPassageTranslation: Neighbours, friends, troublemakers — you know who you are. Twenty years ago I opened this bakery with a sack of flour and no idea what I was doing. Today I leave it with no flour, thousands of memories and, if I'm honest, the same no idea. This neighbourhood gave me three things: a patience I didn't have, questions I couldn't answer, and customers who, in the end, answered them themselves. That is the secret nobody tells you: you don't sell bread. You lend confidence until people realise — and realise they do — that it was theirs all along. Thank you, and mind the step on your way out.

en_es_c2_2_read_final.title: Reading: La última lección
en_es_c2_2_read_final.helpMemoryIntro: The course's final text: on what fluency really is.

helpMemoryTips.title: Fluency = choice
helpMemoryTips.text: Pausing where the thought pauses and walking around the missing word: exactly what you already know how to do.

en_es_c2_2_read_final.readingTitle: Qué es de verdad la fluidez
en_es_c2_2_read_final.readingPassage: Existe el mito persistente de que la fluidez es velocidad. No lo es. La fluidez es elección. El hablante fluido no es el que nunca pausa, sino el que pausa donde pausa el pensamiento; no el que conoce todas las palabras, sino el que, al faltarle una, la rodea con tanta gracia que nadie nota el hueco. Los estudiantes persiguen a los nativos como si la imitación fuera el destino. Pero la mente bilingüe no es copia de nada: es una tercera cosa, con geometría propia — una mente capaz de mirar un idioma desde el balcón del otro. Eso es lo que has construido, módulo a módulo. Nadie puede quitártelo y — aquí va el último secreto — nadie más puede ver cómo se hizo. A los demás les parecerá magia. A ti te parecerá trabajo. Y los dos tendrán razón.
en_es_c2_2_read_final.readingPassageTranslation: There is a persistent myth that fluency is speed. It is not. Fluency is choice. The fluent speaker is not the one who never pauses, but the one who pauses where the thought pauses; not the one who knows every word, but the one who, missing a word, walks around it so gracefully that nobody notices the gap. Learners chase natives as if imitation were the destination. But the bilingual mind is not a copy of anything: it is a third thing, with its own geometry — a mind able to watch one language from the balcony of the other. That is what you have built, module by module. Nobody can take it from you and — here is the last secret — nobody else can see how it was made. To others it will look like magic. To you it will look like work. And both will be right.

readingQuestions.question: ¿Qué es la mente bilingüe según el texto?

en_zh_a1_1_numbers.helpMemoryIntro: Learn ten characters and you can count to 99: eleven is "ten-one" (十一), twenty-two is "two-ten-two" (二十二). It's arithmetic, not memorization.

helpMemoryTips.title: Building-block numbers
helpMemoryTips.text: 11 = 十一 (10+1), 20 = 二十 (2×10), 35 = 三十五 (3×10+5). Every number to 99 is built from 一 to 十 — compare English's eleven, twelve, twenty…

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚠️ 二 vs 两
helpMemoryTips.text: Counting uses 二 (èr): 一, 二, 三. But "two of something" uses 两 (liǎng): 两百 two hundred, and later 两个人 two people.

en_zh_a1_1_pinyin.title: Pinyin: the tricky letters

subjects.english: q = "ch" + smile: qī qǐng qù — seven, please, go
x = soft "sh" + smile: xièxie xiǎo xī — thanks, small, west
zh/ch/sh = tongue curled back: Zhōngguó chī shì
r = a buzzy r, no lip rounding: rén rè Rìběn
b vs p — the puff of air: bàba pà — dad, fear
ü = say "ee", round your lips: nǚ lǜ qù — woman, green, go

en_zh_a1_1_pinyin.helpMemoryIntro: Pinyin uses the letters you know, but a few carry different sounds. Learn only where pinyin differs from English — the rest is free.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚠️ Don't read pinyin as English (Z3)
helpMemoryTips.text: c = "ts" (cats), q = "ch" with a smile, x = soft "sh" with a smile, z = "ds" (kids), zh/ch/sh/r = tongue curled back. "Cài" is tsài, never "kai".

helpMemoryTips.title: b d g: a puff of air, not a voice (Z4)
helpMemoryTips.text: Mandarin b/d/g are gentle, unvoiced p/t/k; p/t/k add a strong puff of air. The contrast is the puff — bā vs pā.

en_zh_a1_1_pronouns.title: Pronouns 我 / 你 / 他 / 她

subjects.display: you and your friends (= you all)
my mum and my aunt (= they, women)

she / her → ____
we / us → ____
you (plural) → ____
they / them → ____
you (polite) → ____
they (all women) → ____
they (things / animals) → ____
everyone / everybody → ____
Tom and I (= we) → ____
you and your friends (= you all) → ____
sentences.english: you and your friends (= you all)

sentences.sentence: my mum and my aunt (= they, women) → ____
sentences.english: my mum and my aunt (= they, women)

en_zh_a1_1_pronouns.helpMemoryIntro: The people words. Good news: they never change form — no "I/me/my" gymnastics. 们 turns people-words plural.

helpMemoryTips.title: The 们 plural
helpMemoryTips.text: 我 I → 我们 we; 你 you → 你们 you all; 他 he → 他们 they. 们 works on people only — nouns themselves have no plural at all (Z9).

helpMemoryTips.title: 他 and 她 sound the same
helpMemoryTips.text: Both are tā. In speech, gender comes for free — only writing distinguishes 他 (he) from 她 (she).

en_zh_a1_1_read_tom.title: Reading: 我叫汤姆
en_zh_a1_1_read_tom.helpMemoryIntro: Your first Chinese text — meet Tom, the course's hero. Read the characters first; pinyin and English wait behind the info button.

helpMemoryTips.title: Read for shapes you know
helpMemoryTips.text: You already know 我, 是, 人, 好. Anchor on familiar characters and guess the rest from context — that's real Chinese reading.

en_zh_a1_1_read_tom.readingPassage: 你好！我叫汤姆，我是英国人。我是学生，我学习中文。我的老师姓王，她是中国人。王老师很好。很高兴认识你！
en_zh_a1_1_read_tom.readingPassageTranslation:
Nǐ hǎo! Wǒ jiào Tāngmǔ, wǒ shì Yīngguó rén. Wǒ shì xuésheng, wǒ xuéxí Zhōngwén. Wǒ de lǎoshī xìng Wáng, tā shì Zhōngguó rén. Wáng lǎoshī hěn hǎo. Hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ!

Hello! My name is Tom, and I'm British. I'm a student and I study Chinese. My teacher's surname is Wang; she's Chinese. Teacher Wang is very nice. Nice to meet you!

en_zh_a1_1_shi.title: 是 — linking nouns (only!)

sentences.sentence: I am a student. → 我____学生。
He is Chinese. → 他____中国人。
She is my friend. → 她____我的朋友。
I am NOT a teacher. → 我____老师。
This is tea. → 这____茶。
They are students. (no plural, no "are"!) → 他们____学生。
You are a teacher. → 你____老师。
We are friends. → 我们____朋友。
That is water. → 那____水。
He is NOT a student. → 他____学生。
This is my teacher. → 这____我的老师。
That is NOT tea. → 那____茶。
She is a doctor. → 她____医生。
I am British. → 我____英国人。
They are NOT teachers. → 他们____老师。

en_zh_a1_1_shi.helpMemoryIntro: 是 shì is "to be" between two nouns: 我是学生 — I am a student. It never changes form (no am/is/are!), and note: no "a/an" needed either.

helpMemoryTips.title: One form, forever
helpMemoryTips.text: 我是, 你是, 他是, 我们是 — all just 是. No conjugation exists in Chinese (Z9). Negate with 不: 我不是老师.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚠️ 是 links NOUNS only (Z10 preview)
helpMemoryTips.text: She is tall = 她很高 — no 是! Adjectives work like verbs in Chinese. 是 + adjective (她是高 ✗) is the classic English-speaker error. The next module drills this.

en_zh_a1_1_speak_intro.title: Speaking: introduce yourself

subjects.english: Wǒ jiào Tāngmǔ. — My name is Tom.
Wǒ shì Yīngguó rén. — I'm British.
Nǐ jiào shénme míngzi? — What's your name?
Hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ. — Nice to meet you.
Nǐ hǎo ma? — How are you?
Wǒ hěn hǎo, xièxie. — I'm fine, thanks.

en_zh_a1_1_speak_intro.helpMemoryIntro: Your first conversation — listen and repeat, copying the tones.

helpMemoryTips.title: Copy the melody, not just the sounds
helpMemoryTips.text: Shadow the voice: hum the pitch pattern first, then add the consonants and vowels. Tone is half the word (Z1).

en_zh_a1_1_tone_pairs.title: Tone pairs & the 你好 rule

subjects.english: hěn hǎo → say "hén hǎo" — very good
wǒ yě hěn hǎo — I'm fine too (a sandhi chain!)

en_zh_a1_1_tone_pairs.helpMemoryIntro: Real words come in tone pairs — and one pair changes: two 3rd tones in a row can't both dip, so the first one rises. 你好 is really ní hǎo.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚠️ Two dips can't dance (Z2)
helpMemoryTips.text: 3rd + 3rd → 2nd + 3rd. 你好 nǐ hǎo → ní hǎo, 很好 hěn hǎo → hén hǎo. Pinyin still writes the original tones — your mouth makes the switch.

helpMemoryTips.title: Drill in pairs
helpMemoryTips.text: Words live as two-syllable teams. Practicing pairs (1+2, 2+4, 3+3…) trains your ear faster than single syllables.

en_zh_a1_1_tones.title: The four tones

subjects.english: mā má mǎ mà — mother · hemp · horse · scold
1st tone (high & flat): mā gāo tiān sān
3rd tone (the low dip): mǎ hǎo wǒ nǐ
4th tone (sharp fall "No!"): mà shì qù dà
Neutral tone (the 2nd syllable relaxes): māma xièxie wǒmen
Māma mà mǎ. — Mum scolds the horse. (All one sound, mā-ma-mà-mǎ!)

en_zh_a1_1_tones.helpMemoryIntro: In Mandarin, pitch is part of the word: mā, má, mǎ and mà are four different words. Listen and copy the melody exactly — the tone matters as much as the letters.

helpMemoryTips.title: Tone gestures
helpMemoryTips.text: 1st = sing it flat and high (a doctor's "aaah"). 2nd = rising "huh?". 3rd = a low, skeptical dip ("we-ell…"). 4th = a sharp "No!". Say the gesture, and the tone follows.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚠️ Tones are not optional (Z1)
helpMemoryTips.text: English uses pitch for attitude; Mandarin uses it for identity. 买 mǎi = buy, 卖 mài = sell — get the tone wrong and you say the opposite word.

sentences.sentence: What does she eat? → 她吃____？

en_zh_a1_1_what_who.helpMemoryIntro: 什么 = what, 谁 = who. The question word sits exactly where the answer will sit — nothing moves to the front.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚠️ The question word stays put (Z12)
helpMemoryTips.text: English fronts "what": WHAT do you buy? Chinese keeps it in the answer's slot: 你买**什么**？(you buy WHAT?). Answer: 你买茶 — same shape.

helpMemoryTips.title: Swap-in trick
helpMemoryTips.text: Take the answer sentence and swap the unknown for 什么/谁: 她是我的老师 → 她是**谁**？

en_zh_a1_2_bu.helpMemoryIntro: 不 bù makes things negative and sits right before the verb or adjective: 我不忙 — I'm not busy. (Only 有 refuses it and takes 没.)

helpMemoryTips.title: 不 + verb/adjective
helpMemoryTips.text: 不是 is not, 不去 doesn't go, 不忙 not busy. One word, one slot — no "don't/doesn't/isn't" zoo (Z9).

helpMemoryTips.title: 不 changes tone before a 4th tone
helpMemoryTips.text: bù + 4th tone → bú: 不是 bú shì, 不累 bú lèi. Your ear probably does it already — now you know why.

en_zh_a1_2_colours.title: Colours & describing

subjects.display: My car is blue. (colour as the whole predicate: 是…的)
What colour is your cup? (what-colour = 什么颜色)

en_zh_a1_2_colours.helpMemoryIntro: Colours end in 色 sè ("colour"): 红色 red, 蓝色 blue. Describing a noun puts the colour in front with 的: 红色的车.

helpMemoryTips.title: Description before the noun (Z19)
helpMemoryTips.text: 红色**的**车 a red car, 大**的**桌子 the big table — description + 的 + noun, always in that order.

en_zh_a1_2_de.helpMemoryIntro: 的 de is the possessive clip: 我的书 = my book, 老师的茶 = the teacher's tea. Close relationships and family often drop it: 我妈妈.

helpMemoryTips.title: Owner + 的 + thing (Z19)
helpMemoryTips.text: Whatever describes a noun comes BEFORE it, clipped on with 的. This little word later carries whole relative clauses — the habit starts here.

helpMemoryTips.title: Family drops 的
helpMemoryTips.text: 我妈妈 (my mum), 我家 (my home), 我朋友 (my friend) — with close people the 的 usually disappears.

en_zh_a1_2_dict_family.title: Dictation: my family

subjects.english: There are four people in my family.
I don't have a younger sister.
How many people are in your family?

en_zh_a1_2_dict_family.helpMemoryIntro: Listen and type with your pinyin keyboard. Watch for the measure words 口, 个 and 只 — English ears love to skip them.

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚠️ Don't drop the measure word (Z11)
helpMemoryTips.text: You will hear 一个哥哥, 一只猫, 四口人 — the little word between number and noun is obligatory. Type what you hear, not what English would say.

en_zh_a1_2_family.title: Family words

sentences.sentence: older brother → ____

en_zh_a1_2_family.helpMemoryIntro: Chinese family words are precise: older and younger siblings get different words. The doubled syllables (妈妈, 爸爸) are easy to say and hear.

helpMemoryTips.title: Older/younger is built in
helpMemoryTips.text: 哥哥 older brother vs 弟弟 younger brother; 姐姐 older sister vs 妹妹 younger sister. There is no plain word for just "brother".

helpMemoryTips.title: The neutral second syllable
helpMemoryTips.text: In 妈妈, 爸爸, 哥哥… the second syllable relaxes to a neutral tone: māma, bàba, gēge.

en_zh_a1_2_hen.title: Adjectives take 很, never 是

subjects.display: Chinese tea is good to drink. (tasty)

This cup of tea is REALLY tasty. (stress with 真)

My home is EXTREMELY far. (stress with 非常)
Her younger brother is short. (opposite of 高)

en_zh_a1_2_hen.helpMemoryIntro: To say "she is tall", Chinese drops "is" and glues the adjective on with 很: 她很高. Adjectives behave like verbs — they need no copula.

helpMemoryTips.title: 很 is the glue, not "very"
helpMemoryTips.text: Plain 她很高 just means "she's tall" — this 很 is nearly empty. To actually stress it, use 真 (really) or 非常 (extremely).

helpMemoryTips.title: ⚠️ 是 + adjective is the classic error (Z10)
helpMemoryTips.text: 她是高 ✗ — 是 links nouns only. And a bare 她高 sounds like a comparison ("SHE's the tall one"). Default shape: subject + 很 + adjective.
